body.statement:
Fix \(m=|\mathcal A|\) and a known \(J\) with \(2\leq J\leq m\). For every \(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{face}}\), the anchor-star recovery map is well-defined and
\[
 \Phi(p)=\theta_J=(\nu_1^\top,\ldots,\nu_J^\top,\tau^\top)^\top
 \in\mathbb R^{(J+1)(m+1)}.
\]
Throughout \(\mathcal F(p)\), in the common descending cycle-product order, the formulas recover \(\alpha_j^d>0\), \(s_j^d\), every active row of \(Q_j\) and \(R_j^d\), the complete unnormalized component law of \((Z,X_0,X_1,X_2,X_3)\) on \(\{X_1\in\mathcal A\}\),
\[
 \nu_j=s_j^1Q_j(R_j^1-R_j^0),\qquad
 \eta_j=\nu_j/\alpha_j^1,
 \qquad \tau=\sum_{j=1}^J\nu_j.
\]
Moreover \(\pi_j^d\geq\alpha_j^d>0\) is derived from anchor-star nonsingularity, rather than assumed. Four anchor slices determine the spectral basis, while the \(2m-1\) observable anchor-star slices transport recovery to all active states. Units with \(X_1=e\) have zero treatment effect by no anticipation and absorption. Without the no-date-\(1\)-absorption condition, the theorem does not identify \(\pi_j^d\) or the full conditional \(\tau_j\). No time homogeneity is required. Only four waves \(X_0,\ldots,X_3\) are required; if a fifth wave is observed it may be marginalized out.
body.justification: This is the field-level four-wave identification theorem: it transports a four-anchor spectral basis over all active states for fixed known \(J\leq m\), derives type positivity, and proves the aggregate-versus-full-conditional frontier.
body.gap: Adjacent reconstruction theorems do not combine a common absorbing boundary, \(2m-1\) selected anchor-star minors, four-wave time-varying causal paths, and the initial-absorber effect decomposition.
body.consumer: An analyst may marginalize any fifth wave and report latent-type contributions and the aggregate when the four-wave anchor-star guard passes, even if full latent allocation of already-exited units is unavailable.
body.proof_tex:
Fix \(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{face}}\) and \(d\in\{0,1\}\).  Assumption \(\texttt{ass:cohort-overlap}\) gives \(P(D=d)>0\), so every cohort-conditional probability below is defined.  For \(x,y\in\mathcal A\), the factors in \(\texttt{def:observed-slices}\) have dimensions
\[
 B_x^{d,\mathcal A}\in\mathbb R_+^{m\times J},\qquad
 D_{xy}\in\mathbb R_+^{J\times J},\qquad
 C_y^d\in\mathbb R_+^{J\times(m+1)},                                    \tag{1}
\]
and stochasticity gives \(C_y^d\mathbf1_{m+1}=\mathbf1_J\).  By \(\texttt{ass:consistency}\) and \(\texttt{ass:no-anticipation}\), the observed coordinates through date \(2\) equal the corresponding coordinates of the realized potential path.  The conditional first-order Markov factorization in \(\texttt{ass:markov-paths}\), and the common date-two transition in \(\texttt{ass:common-date-two-transition}\), give, for \(u,x,y\in\mathcal A\) and \(v\in\mathcal S\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 A_{xy}^d[u,v]
 &=\sum_{j=1}^J P(X_0=u,X_1=x,Z=j\mid D=d)
 Q_j[x,y]P(X_3=v\mid X_2=y,Z=j,D=d)\\
 &=\sum_{j=1}^J B_x^{d,\mathcal A}[u,j]Q_j[x,y]C_y^d[j,v].
\end{aligned}                                                              \tag{2}
\]
Thus
\[
 A_{xy}^d=B_x^{d,\mathcal A}D_{xy}C_y^d,
 \qquad M_{xy}^d=B_x^{d,\mathcal U}D_{xy}C_y^{d,\mathcal V}.              \tag{3}
\]

Every factor in the second equality of (3) is square of order \(J\).  Assumption \(\texttt{ass:four-slice-rank}\) makes \(M_{x_0y}^d\) nonsingular for every \(y\in\mathcal A\).  The determinant product in (3) therefore makes \(B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}\), every \(D_{x_0y}\), and every \(C_y^{d,\mathcal V}\) nonsingular.  The same assumption makes \(M_{xy_0}^d\) nonsingular for every \(x\in\mathcal A\), whence every \(B_x^{d,\mathcal U}\) and every \(D_{xy_0}\) is nonsingular.  Since diagonal entries of \(D_{xy}\) are transition probabilities,
\[
 Q_j[x_0,y]>0,\qquad Q_j[x,y_0]>0                                         \tag{4}
\]
for all \(j,x,y\).  These inequalities justify all divisions below.  Notice that \(M_{x_1y_1}^d\) is multiplied but never inverted.

Substitution of (3) into the definition of \(K^d\), followed by cancellation of adjacent invertible factors, yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
 K^d
 &=B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}D_{x_0y_0}C_{y_0}^{d,\mathcal V}
 (B_{x_1}^{d,\mathcal U}D_{x_1y_0}C_{y_0}^{d,\mathcal V})^{-1}\\
 &\quad\cdot B_{x_1}^{d,\mathcal U}D_{x_1y_1}C_{y_1}^{d,\mathcal V}
 (B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}D_{x_0y_1}C_{y_1}^{d,\mathcal V})^{-1}\\
 &=B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}\operatorname{diag}_{1\leq j\leq J}
 \left\{\frac{Q_j[x_0,y_0]Q_j[x_1,y_1]}
 {Q_j[x_1,y_0]Q_j[x_0,y_1]}\right\}
 (B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U})^{-1}.
\end{aligned}                                                              \tag{5}
\]
The displayed cross-ratios are the eigenvalues \(\rho_j^d\).  They are distinct and decreasingly labelled by \(\texttt{ass:simple-cycle-spectrum}\).  If \(E_j\) is diagonal with sole nonzero entry \(E_j[j,j]=1\), direct evaluation of the Lagrange polynomial at the diagonal matrix in (5) proves
\[
 P_j^d=\prod_{k\ne j}\frac{K^d-\rho_k^dI_J}{\rho_j^d-\rho_k^d}
 =B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}E_j(B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U})^{-1}.                  \tag{6}
\]
Summing the latent label in the definition of the observed predecessor vector gives
\[
 m_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}=B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}\mathbf1_J.
\]
Combining this equality with (6) fixes both eigenvector scale and sign:
\[
 P_j^dm_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}=B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}[:,j].                 \tag{7}
\]
Consequently the first matrix built by \(\texttt{def:recovery-map}\) is the true \(B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}\).

Equations (2), (4), and (7) imply, for every \(y\in\mathcal A\),
\[
 F_y^d=D_{x_0y}C_y^d,\qquad
 q_{x_0y}^d=F_y^d\mathbf1_{m+1}=D_{x_0y}\mathbf1_J.                       \tag{8}
\]
Every coordinate of the last vector is positive by (4); hence row-sum normalization gives exactly
\[
 \operatorname{diag}(q_{x_0y}^d)^{-1}F_y^d=C_y^d.                         \tag{9}
\]
The selected minor \(C_{y_0}^{d,\mathcal V}\) is nonsingular, so \(C_{y_0}^d\) has row rank \(J\), and therefore \(C_{y_0}^d(C_{y_0}^d)^\top\) is positive definite.  It follows from (2) and (9) that
\[
\begin{aligned}
 W_x^d
 &=A_{xy_0}^{d,\mathcal U,\mathcal S}(C_{y_0}^d)^\top
 \{C_{y_0}^d(C_{y_0}^d)^\top\}^{-1}\\
 &=B_x^{d,\mathcal U}D_{xy_0}.
\end{aligned}                                                              \tag{10}
\]
This matrix is nonsingular.  Since \(m_x^{d,\mathcal U}=B_x^{d,\mathcal U}\mathbf1_J\),
\[
 c_x^d=(W_x^d)^{-1}m_x^{d,\mathcal U}=D_{xy_0}^{-1}\mathbf1_J>0,
 \qquad W_x^d\operatorname{diag}(c_x^d)=B_x^{d,\mathcal U}.              \tag{11}
\]

When \(J<m\), the selected rows alone do not contain all predecessor masses.  Restricting (2) to rows \(\mathcal A\) and columns \(\mathcal V\), then using (9) and (11), gives the required full-row transport:
\[
\begin{aligned}
 A_{xy_0}^{d,\mathcal A,\mathcal V}(C_{y_0}^{d,\mathcal V})^{-1}
 \operatorname{diag}(c_x^d)
 &=B_x^{d,\mathcal A}D_{xy_0}\operatorname{diag}(c_x^d)\\
 &=B_x^{d,\mathcal A}.
\end{aligned}                                                              \tag{12}
\]
For arbitrary \(x,y\in\mathcal A\), equations (2), (9), and (11) now give
\[
 q_{xy}^d=(B_x^{d,\mathcal U})^{-1}
 A_{xy}^{d,\mathcal U,\mathcal S}\mathbf1_{m+1}
 =D_{xy}\mathbf1_J.                                                        \tag{13}
\]
Thus \(q_{xy}^d[j]=Q_j[x,y]\), including possibly zero non-anchor transitions.  Row stochasticity identifies
\[
 Q_j[x,e]=1-\sum_{y\in\mathcal A}Q_j[x,y],                                \tag{14}
\]
and \(\texttt{ass:absorbing-exit}\) supplies the absorbing exit row.  Equation (9) identifies every active row of the factual first-post matrix \(R_j^d\), and absorption again supplies its exit row.

Summing the recovered predecessor probabilities gives
\[
 s_j^d[x]=\mathbf1_m^\top B_x^{d,\mathcal A}[:,j]
 =P(Z=j,X_1=x\mid D=d),\qquad
 \alpha_j^d=\sum_{x\in\mathcal A}s_j^d[x].                              \tag{15}
\]
The nonnegative square matrix \(B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}\) is nonsingular, so each of its columns is nonzero and has strictly positive column sum.  Consequently
\[
 \alpha_j^d\geq\mathbf1_J^\top B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}[:,j]>0,
 \qquad
 \pi_j^d=\alpha_j^d+P(Z=j,X_1=e\mid D=d)\geq\alpha_j^d>0.                \tag{16}
\]
Thus type overlap is a consequence of the observable rank hypothesis rather than an additional assumption.

Equations (2) and (8)--(15) recover the complete unnormalized component law on \(\{X_1\in\mathcal A\}\).  Indeed, \(\texttt{ass:absorbing-exit}\) implies \(X_1\in\mathcal A\Rightarrow X_0\in\mathcal A\), and for \(u,x,y\in\mathcal A\), \(v\in\mathcal S\), its conditional-on-cohort cell mass is
\[
 B_x^{d,\mathcal A}[u,j]Q_j[x,y]R_j^d[y,v],                               \tag{17}
\]
whereas for \(y=e\) it is
\[
 B_x^{d,\mathcal A}[u,j]Q_j[x,e]\mathbf1\{v=e\}.
\]
In particular, positivity in (16) makes the following conditional law well defined:
\[
 P(X_2\in\cdot\mid D=d,Z=j,X_1\in\mathcal A)
 =\frac{s_j^dQ_j}{\alpha_j^d}.                                             \tag{18}
\]

Because the cross-ratios in (5) involve only the cohort-common matrices \(Q_j\), their strict descending order is common across cohorts.  By consistency, \(R_j^0=U_j\) on active rows.  No anticipation makes the treated cohort's \(X_2\) the same under both potential paths, while \(\texttt{ass:common-first-post-untreated-transition}\) makes its untreated continuation equal to \(U_j=R_j^0\).  If \(X_1=e\), no anticipation and absorption imply \(X_3(1)=X_3(0)=e\), so this event contributes zero.  Iterated expectation using (18) therefore proves the causal, rather than definitional, identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \nu_j
 &=E\!\left[\mathbf1\{Z=j\}
 \{\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(1))-\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(0))\}
 \mid D=1\right]\\
 &=s_j^1Q_j(R_j^1-R_j^0).
\end{aligned}                                                              \tag{19}
\]
Since \(\alpha_j^1>0\), the same calculation conditional on the active event yields
\[
 \eta_j=\frac{\nu_j}{\alpha_j^1}.                                         \tag{20}
\]
Finite additivity over the known support \(Z\in\{1,\ldots,J\}\) gives
\[
 \tau=\sum_{j=1}^J\nu_j.                                                   \tag{21}
\]
Equations (19)--(21) are exactly \(\Phi(p)=\theta_J\).  Every operation used only the observed four-wave law and the declared nonzero ranks, eigengaps, and stochastic normalizations, so the same derivation holds for every \(\widetilde P\in\mathcal F(p)\).  The four matrices occurring in (5) determine the spectral basis; the \(2m-1\) distinct selected anchor-star slices in (8)--(13) transport that basis to all active states.  Neither time homogeneity nor a transition after date \(3\) was used.  Only the four waves \(X_0,\ldots,X_3\) are required; an observed fifth wave may be marginalized out.
